newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-KLM SAYS BA BLOCKS NEW SERVICE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-KLM SAYS BA BLOCKS NEW SERVICE.

text.p: Dutch carrier KLM on Tuesday accused rival British Airways of seeking to block a new London-Amsterdam-Nairobi service by KLM's 26 percent-owned partner Kenya Airways .

KLM spokesman Hans Leijte said British authorities had refused Kenya Airways permission to re-route its London-Nairobi service through Amsterdam, adding that KLM believed this was due to behind-the-scenes pressure from British Airways.
"Kenya Airways has been refused permission to fly to Amsterdam from London," Leijte said. "We believe this is due to obstruction from British Airways. It's pure bedevilment."

But the British carrier dismissed the complaint, saying nothing was settled yet and the issue was all part of the cut and thrust of governments negotiating landing rights for their airlines under the global system of bilateral aviation treaties.
"Kenya went to the British authorities and said they wanted to have new routing rights between Amsterdam and London," a spokeswoman for British Airways said.
"As is normal with bilaterals we have said 'right, let's get round the table and see what sort of proposals we can come up with' and that is what is going on at the moment."
Britain's Department of Transport (DOT) said its negotiators were meeting with their counterparts in Nairobi this week.

"There are various issues about air services between the two countries that are under discussion in Kenya at the moment and as is usual BA has a part to play...but it's fairly standard procedure," a spokeswoman for the DOT said.
Kenya Airways previously operated a London-Nairobi service with a stopover in Frankfurt.
Under the new partnership with KLM, Kenya Airways flights to Frankfurt and Zurich have been scrapped with the aim of substituting an Amsterdam stopover, Leijte said.
In turn KLM planned to reduce its Nairobi service from four flights a week to three.
The Kenya Airways service to Nairobi would be subject to code-sharing, meaning it would operate under a KLM flight number from Amsterdam.
Leijte said the change of stopover would not affect the existing situation on the highly competitive London-Amsterdam route, as all passengers out of London were bound for Nairobi.
"What we find particularly irksome about this business is that the Netherlands and Britain have always been in the forefront of European deregulation," Leijte said.
He said Kenyan and British authorities were meeting to discuss the issue today and tomorrow (Wednesday) whereas the new London-Amsterdam-Nairobi service was already scheduled to start on Friday.

KLM acquired its Kenya Airways stake for $26 million in January, saying the buy would help bolster its position in Africa. At the time British Airways was also in the running for a Kenya Airways stake.
